So I had this interesting conversation recently with a very senior IT leader at one of SaaStr Fund’s portfolio companies that sells into enterprises, especially larger ones (think $100m+ ACV).  They are doing well now, but when they started off, they didn’t really understand how to sell up.  To the CIO level, the VP level, the business process owners.
A few years back, we did a deep dive on “how to sell to CIOs” with the CIO of Workday,
a great session you can watch here:
But my experience is most founders aren’t sure how to do it.   They want their product to be used by everyone across an enterprise, ideally starting with the CEO and going all the way down through sales reps and engineers.  But most CEOs don’t know enough to buy software themselves, no matter how cool it is.  And most CIOs will want nothing to do with anyone who hasn’t worked in tech for decades, unless they’ve been truly vetted as part of their own network.  That leaves VPs of Sales and Engineering … often the #2 and #3 folks in any org.  Not exactly what many start-ups want to try to sell to.
The thing is, if you can get past them — they’ll almost always buy more than just your core app.  More features, more seats, more modules, etc.  So there is real revenue there, even with just an 8-person team.  It’s hard to close big deals without a brand behind you.  Or so it seems.
Here was our experience at Adobe Sign / EchoSign:
We closed some pretty big deals early on ourselves, but once we got past a few $500k-$1m deals, we needed a partner with us.  We added a local reseller, and then later, a channel manager, and then eventually, a global channel director.  Later still, we hired a Global Channel Head from Salesforce to build out a full channel strategy.

A great talk with Bill McDermott at Dreamforce here:
Can your startup sell to a CIO if you are tiny?
Of course you can!  But … will they buy from you? That’s different.
The thing is, almost all start-ups selling to developers have figured this out. Developers don’t care how many people there are on your team. They just want solutions that work fast and well.
But enterprise buyers, especially larger ones? They often do. At least, for some products. Not always. And not as much these days as even 24 months ago. But still enough to matter.
I remember back in the day when I was a VP in charge of buying $20m+ worth of software each year. Our biggest vendor had literally hundreds and hundreds of employees. We met with them every week. It was our job to know their product cold, so we could tell our bosses exactly what we needed.
We never did business with anyone smaller than us. Period. Unless it truly added value and solved a problem. Then sometimes, yes, even then. Sometimes we’d try new vendors if the CEO or founders were very smart and really good, like SaaS veterans (e.g., from Salesforce).
Even today,
SaaStr Fund
only invests in startups with proven leaders at CEO and/or co-CEO. There’s no way those folks would get anywhere without strong teams behind them.
Still, I think most of us learn to be agile once we are successful. Most CEOs that fail early learn to build big teams later. And most winners figure out how to work around limited resources by getting smarter and more efficient.
So can a small company close a large deal? Of course. Many times.

I am so excited that we have four amazing speakers today talking about enterprise sales for SaaS startups, which I think is one of the most misunderstood parts of selling into big companies, especially as you get bigger. And also because I know this room has people who are interested in going upmarket and selling in the enterprise, right?
Can you sell your product to the CIO when you're eight person company? Well, yes, you can. But only if you understand something called the social contract. What's the social contract? It's what you owe them before they ever even buy your product. Let me share with you three things that I learned from these incredible CEOs of Workday, DISH, and BDP all spoke at Demo last year.
[01:00]
The first thing I learned was how important trust was between vendors and customers. There's this quote that Aneel said from Workday where he says "I don't need to be friends with my vendor, but I do want to trust him." That means I'm gonna go out on a limb for him."
This is super important. When I look back at the deals I lost early on, there were two types of deals that always fell apart. One was just the usual suspects—lack of features, didn't solve their problem—but another category that failed more often than you'd expect was the deal where the customer felt like they got screwed by us, the seller. Either through some sleazy tactic or just outright lying. We've talked about this. I used to say that a bad salesperson will tell you anything to close the deal. Now, I just say that any time someone lies to you, walk away. Because once you lie, you'll keep lying, and then you'll lose the respect of everyone else involved. So remember, it's all about trust.
[02:03]
Another great piece of advice came from Tony Hsieh from Zappos. He gave this wonderful analogy that I use all the time. He said that every single day, your customers are asking themselves, "Should I renew?" They're doing this calculation: Am I happy enough? Do I see value in this relationship? Should I stay?

We
last looked in on Monday.com at $240m ARR
, but it’s grown so incredibly quickly, and so effectively, it’s worth checking in again at $400,000,000 in ARR.
Because at $400,000,000 in ARR …  Monday is growing a stunning 91% (!) year-over-year.  Goodness gracious!
5 Interesting Learnings:

#1.  Revenue up 91%, Customer Count Up “Just” 34%.  The math of going upmarket
.  I personally get a little worried when this ratio falls below 2:1, if only because sometimes upsell can mask lower growth in new accounts.  The real story with Monday is going upmarket.  $50k+ customers are up 200%, to 793 from 264 a year ago.  That’s a key driver to Monday’s hyper-growth as it approaches $500,000,000 in ARR.
#2.  10+ Users the Sweet Spot now
.  As part of going upmarket, Monday’s 10+ seat customers are now 72% of total revenue, up from 63% just a year ago.  Asana has seen similar dynamics, but Monday seems to be going upmarket even faster than Asana.

#7.  Monday.com is growing 68% (!) at $550m in ARR.  No SMB deceleration here!
Not much, at least.  Monday’s growth has slowed a little bit, but in absolute terms, the growth is just incredible even now.

.

with some pretty incredible numbers, especially considering just how competitive the space is.
At $240m in ARR, they are growing a stunning 85% year-over-year!  And that’s with direct and indirect competition from Asana, Atlassian, Clickup, Wrike, Smartsheet, Notion and so many others.
Pretty incredible for a product that just launched in 2014.
Whoa.
5 Interesting Learnings:
#1.  121% NRR from 10+ seat customers, 107% overall, ~85% from smallest customers.
This is a super-helpful breakdown for anyone selling to customers both smaller and larger.  65% of its revenue comes from 10+ seat deals and they have 121% NRR.  The remaining 35% is from smaller deals.  For those to average to 107%, NRR is likely around 85% for self-service and < 10 seat deals (about the same as
Squarespace
).
So those seem like good yardsticks to shoot for if you sell to SMBs of all shapes and sizes and are somewhat like Monday.  The tiniest of customers may have only 85% NRR.  But once you cross 10 seats, you should start to see the benefits of account growth and 120% NRR like Monday.
